fixes.explanation: Kindness it is, baker. David, Israel's king, says, “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me.” Hanun is the new king of the Ammonites, and David wants to answer kindness with kindness.

Not this time, friend. The text says David did send some of his servants to console Hanun concerning his father. Hanun is the new Ammonite king, and his father has died. So this is a visit meant as comfort, and David sends his own servants to deliver it.
That would be a clean sweep, friend, but the text says half. Hanun shaved off half of each man's beard. These are David's servants, who came to console him, so I'll just say what the text says.

False is right, baker. When the Ammonites realized they had become a stench to David, they hired soldiers. They didn't send a gift. Their answer to becoming a stench to David was to bring in an army, and that's all the text tells us.

Yes, baker. Joab picks some of Israel's best men to face the Arameans, then puts the rest under his brother Abishai to face the Ammonites. One army, two fronts. Joab saw the battle lines before him and behind him and set up his troops.

Joab doesn't wait, baker. The text shows him selecting men to array against the Arameans and putting the rest under Abishai. David sent Joab and the entire army of mighty men. Nothing in these verses has Joab waiting for anyone.
Best, baker. The text says Joab “…selected some of the best men of Israel…” and lined them up against the Arameans. Abishai gets the rest of the troops, who face the Ammonites.
Newest isn't the word, friend. The text says Joab selected some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Arameans. The rest of the troops go under Abishai.

True, baker. Joab says, “Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God.” He says it right after telling Abishai how they'll rescue each other. That's a pep talk with real stakes behind it.

Not so, baker. When Joab and his troops advance to fight the Arameans, the text says they “…fled before him.” So the Arameans don't hold their ground here. When the Ammonites saw that the Arameans had fled, they fled too (2 Samuel 10:14).
David does cross the Jordan and go to Helam, baker, but the Arameans don't push anybody back. The text says they “…fled before Israel…” That's the opposite of pushing Israel back.
The Ammonites went into their city earlier in the passage, baker. What the text says these kings did is make peace with Israel and become subject to them. That's the answer, not hiding.
Not anymore, baker. The last line of the passage says, “So the Arameans were afraid to help the Ammonites anymore.” That comes after the kings made peace with Israel and became subject to them.
False, baker. The text says, “So the Arameans were afraid to help the Ammonites anymore.” Afraid is the word the text uses. The kings had made peace with Israel by then.
